newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seven years of shrinking economy hit N.Korea - Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Seven years of shrinking economy hit N.Korea - Seoul.

text.p: North Korea's economy shrank for the seventh straight year in 1996, the South Korean government said on Thursday.
A report by the ministry of national unification, which monitors North Korea, said the North's economy contracted by an estimated three percent last year after negative growth of 4.5 percent in 1995.
"North Korea's food shortage is worsening as the shortfall keeps accumulating," a ministry official said.

North Korea's food harvest totalled 3.69 million tonnes last year, up from 3.45 million tonnes from 1995 but below the average annual crop of 4.14 million tonnes, the report said, without giving details of how the average was calculated.
The official said the United Nations' World Food Programme's estimate of a 2.3 million tonne food shortage in North Korea this year was conservative.

Catherine Bertini, WFP executive director, said on Tuesday at the end of a trip to North Korea that the presence of thin, lethargic children there indicated that a famine that could strike the impoverished state as early as this month.

An influential South Korean newspaper on Wednesday quoted North Korean leader Kim Jong-il as saying that anarchy could soon reign his nation because of an acute food shortage that has even hit the military.
Kim held Communist Party and government officials responsible for "a state of anarchy being created because of food problems today", the Chosun Ilbo said.
The daily, reputed to have many sources within the Seoul government, said Kim made the remarks in a speech on December 7 in Pyongyang. It did not say how it obtained the speech.
"People are found everywhere scrounging for food," Kim was quoted as saying. "Stations and trains are crowded with people looking for food. You see heartbreaking scenes everywhere."

The unification ministry report said the bulk of North Korea's production facilities were idled because of a serious energy shortage. Less than 30 percent of plants in the Stalinist nation were in operation in 1996.
Pyongyang's foreign trade totalled $1.07 billion in 1996, down 5.3 percent from the previous year.
